transcript.text: Price Ceilings
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-19
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding ceilings and analyze shortages and rationing.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A price ceiling sets a legal maximum price and is binding only when it lies below the market equilibrium price. A binding ceiling keeps price from rising to equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage develops. A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the legal maximum price with the market equilibrium price.
A ceiling below equilibrium is binding and creates excess demand.
At the ceiling price, read quantity demanded and quantity supplied; their difference is the shortage.
A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not change the market outcome.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to assume that every price ceiling is binding. A price ceiling above equilibrium is not binding. Since $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price, it does not affect the market.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BINDING PRICE CEILING

The horizontal axis is quantity and the vertical axis is price. An upward-sloping supply curve and downward-sloping demand curve intersect at price $30 and quantity 200. Dashed guides also show demand and supply quantities at prices $10, $20, $40, and $50: at $10, supply is 100 and demand is 300; at $20, supply is 150 and demand is 250; at $40, supply is 250 and demand is 150; at $50, supply is 300 and demand is 100.

The market equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. A binding ceiling of $20 holds price below equilibrium; buyers demand 250 units while sellers supply 150. The resulting shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units, so some willing buyers cannot purchase at the controlled price.
CHECK YOURSELF
At a binding price ceiling, Qd = 90 and Qs = 60. What is the shortage?
